questions.stem: A class wants to show how the area of irrigated cropland in a Murray-Darling district has changed between 2005 and 2025. Which geospatial tool is most suitable?
options: Comparing georeferenced satellite images of the district for both years in a GIS
Plotting a line graph of the district's annual rainfall totals in a spreadsheet
Recording GPS coordinates of ten farm gates during a one-day field trip
Building a survey form to ask current farmers about their water allocations
questions.explanation: Change in land cover over time is best measured by comparing georeferenced images of the same area at two dates, because a GIS lets you overlay the layers and calculate the change in area. The rainfall line graph is tempting since it uses a digital tool and covers the same period, but rainfall is a different variable and shows nothing about how much land is irrigated. Match the tool to the variable and the time span the question asks about.

questions.stem: A class measures air temperature at 12 sites with their own thermometers. This data is:
options: secondary data, because the sites were chosen from an existing map
primary data, because the students collected the measurements themselves
secondary data, because the readings were taken using instruments
qualitative data, because the readings describe the conditions at each site
questions.explanation: Primary data is information a geographer gathers first-hand in the field or by their own survey; secondary data has already been collected, processed or published by someone else. Calling the readings 'secondary data, because the readings were taken using instruments' confuses the tool with the source — using a thermometer, GPS or app does not make data second-hand. The cue is simple: ask who generated the number. If it was your class on the day, it is primary.

questions.stem: You need secondary data on how rainfall has changed over 50 years. Which source?
options: Long-term rainfall records published by the Bureau of Meteorology
Rain gauge readings the group takes at school over four weeks
Interviews with three local farmers about this season's crop losses
Photographs the group takes of dry paddocks during a field trip
questions.explanation: Secondary sources are datasets already collected and published by others, and a 50-year trend can only come from records that pre-date the inquiry. 'Rain gauge readings the group takes at school over four weeks' is tempting because rainfall is the right variable, but four weeks of self-collected data is primary and far too short to show change over decades. Match the source to both the time span and the question of who collected it.

questions.stem: Students collect litter counts at 15 coastal sites and record each site's location with a GPS app. Before drawing conclusions, they enter the counts into a spreadsheet, calculate the mean count per 100 m² and plot the sites in GIS software with graduated symbols. This stage of the inquiry is best described as:
options: evaluating sources, because the reliability of the counts is being checked
communicating findings, because the results now appear as a finished map
processing data, because the raw records are organised and represented for analysis
collecting data, because GPS locations are still being added to each record
questions.explanation: Processing is the step between collection and conclusions: sorting, calculating, graphing and mapping raw records so patterns can be seen. 'Communicating findings' is the closest tempting option, but communication happens when the results are presented to an audience with an explanation and conclusion; here the map is a working tool for the students' own analysis. The cue is purpose — a representation made to reveal a pattern is processing, one made to present a conclusion is communicating.

questions.stem: On a climate graph (climograph), how are the two data sets shown?
options: Columns for yearly rainfall, with a line for the town's population change
Columns for average monthly rainfall in millimetres, and a line for temperature
Columns for average monthly temperature, and a line for rainfall in millimetres
Two lines, one for rainfall and one for temperature, on a single axis
questions.explanation: A climograph combines two different variables for the twelve months of the year: rainfall is plotted as columns (a quantity accumulated over each month) and temperature as a line (an average condition that changes continuously), each with its own vertical axis and units. The version with temperature as columns and rainfall as a line reverses the standard convention, so a student reading a real climograph would misread every value. The cue is that anything measured as an accumulated total, like rainfall, is drawn as columns, while an average that flows from month to month is drawn as a line.

questions.stem: Using GIS software, students combine four mapped layers for a region — soil type, average annual rainfall, slope, and distance to a grain terminal — to identify land that meets all four conditions for growing wheat. This use of geospatial technology is best described as:
options: Transect sampling, in which readings are collected in sequence along a single line drawn across the study area
Overlay analysis, in which layers are stacked so the software identifies locations satisfying every criterion at once
Change detection, in which images of the same place from two different dates are compared to measure what has altered
Geocoding, in which written addresses or place names are converted into coordinates so they can be plotted
questions.explanation: The defining power of GIS is that spatially referenced layers can be overlaid so that the software finds the areas where several conditions coincide, which is exactly what suitability mapping requires. Change detection is tempting because it also uses multiple GIS layers, but those layers are the same variable at different dates, whereas here they are four different variables at one time. The cue is what the layers differ by: different dates means change detection, different variables means overlay.

questions.stem: A group maps total tonnes of food produced by each Victorian local government area, shading the highest totals darkest. The very large rural LGAs all appear dark. What is the main problem, and the best fix?
options: Shading is never suitable for numerical information, so the map should use one colour with the tonnage figure labelled inside each LGA
The problem is only the number of shading classes, because using more colour categories always removes the influence of area size on the pattern
Larger LGAs can record bigger totals simply because they cover more land, so the map should show production per hectare to allow fair comparison
Choropleth maps can only display data gathered at single points, so the totals should be redrawn as proportional circles at each LGA centre
questions.explanation: Choropleth maps shade whole areal units, so mapping raw totals confuses the size of the variable with the size of the unit; converting to a rate or density (per hectare, per person) removes that distortion. The suggestion about more shading classes is tempting because class breaks do affect the appearance of a choropleth, but finer classes cannot correct a variable that is inflated by area. The cue is simple: choropleths need rates or densities, not raw counts.

questions.stem: You have income and undernourishment figures for 50 countries. Which graph shows the relationship?
options: A pie chart, one slice per country sized by undernourishment
A climograph, income as bars and undernourishment as a line above
A topographic map, with contour lines at each undernourishment rate
A scatterplot, income on one axis and undernourishment on the other
questions.explanation: A scatterplot is the standard format for showing the relationship between two continuous variables measured for the same set of places, because each point carries both values at once and any trend becomes visible. The pie chart option is tempting because pie charts are common in geography, but a pie shows parts of a single whole (percentage shares) and rates for 50 separate countries do not add to a meaningful whole. The cue is the word 'relationship' or 'tend to': two variables compared across many cases means a scatterplot, while 'share of a total' means a pie or stacked bar.

questions.stem: Students plot GDP per person against life expectancy for 60 countries. The points form a clear positive trend, but three high-income oil-exporting countries sit well below the trend line. Which conclusion is best supported by this graph?
options: Because the trend is strong, life expectancy for any country can be read off exactly from its GDP figure
There is a positive relationship overall, but the outliers show income alone does not determine life expectancy
The graph proves that increasing GDP per person directly causes life expectancy to rise in every country
The three outlying countries indicate measurement errors and should be deleted before the trend is described
questions.explanation: Analysing a scatterplot means describing both the general trend and the points that depart from it; outliers are evidence that other factors, such as how income is distributed or spent on health services, also shape wellbeing. The option claiming the graph proves income causes longer life is the most tempting, but a graph can only show correlation between variables, never establish cause on its own. Remember that outliers are findings to explain, not faults to remove, and a trend describes a general pattern rather than an exact prediction for each place.

questions.stem: A student uses a 30-year record of a country's wheat production to estimate what production might be in 2035, by continuing the established trend beyond the final data point. This technique is called:
options: aggregation
standardisation
extrapolation
interpolation
questions.explanation: Extrapolation means extending an established trend past the last recorded observation to estimate values outside the range of the data, which is how simple forecasts are made. Interpolation is the tempting alternative, but it means estimating a value between two known data points — for example, guessing 2012 production from the 2010 and 2015 figures. Cue: extrapolation goes beyond the data, interpolation stays inside it.

questions.stem: A graph of wheat yield from 1985 to 2025 rises overall with sharp dips. What is the 'trend'?
options: The single highest yield recorded, showing what the country can produce
The difference between each year's yield and the year before it
The average of all the yearly values across the whole record
The general direction the values move, despite year-to-year dips
questions.explanation: A trend is the overall direction of change across a time series; short-term dips caused by drought or disease are fluctuations around that trend, not the trend itself. The tempting wrong choice is the average of all the yearly values — that is a single summary statistic (the mean) and tells you nothing about whether values are rising or falling. The cue is the word 'direction': a trend always has an up, down or steady sense over time, while an average has no direction at all.

questions.stem: Across 80 countries, more mobile phones per person goes with longer life expectancy. Conclude what?
options: Owning phones lengthens life expectancy, since the two rise together
Longer life causes phone ownership, as the cause must be the health one
There is no relationship, since the two are different kinds of measure
The two are positively associated, but this cannot show one causes the other
questions.explanation: Data showing two variables moving together establishes a correlation; a third factor such as national income can raise both, so causation cannot be inferred from the pattern alone. The most tempting wrong option is that owning mobile phones lengthens life expectancy — it reads the correlation as proof of cause, which the data do not support. The cue is to ask whether a plausible third variable could drive both measures before claiming any causal link.

questions.stem: A country records the share of its population that is undernourished: 2005 – 24%, 2010 – 18%, 2015 – 13%, 2020 – 9%. Which forecast for 2025 is best supported by this data?
options: About 13 per cent, because values in a data series tend to return towards the middle figure
About 5 to 6 per cent, continuing the downward trend, though the fall may slow at low levels
About 9 per cent, because the most recent figure is always the safest forecast to use
About 1 per cent, because the percentage has been roughly halving in each five-year period
questions.explanation: The series falls by 6, then 5, then 4 percentage points, so the trend is downward but decelerating; extending it gives a fall of around 3 to 4 points to roughly 5 or 6 per cent. The tempting wrong option is about 9 per cent using the most recent figure — that ignores the clear, consistent downward movement the data show. Check the size of each step before forecasting: here the steps shrink, which is why halving to 1 per cent also badly overshoots.

questions.stem: A group uses 15 years of local rainfall records to draw a straight trend line and forecasts rainfall for 2050 by extending that line. Which criticism most seriously weakens their forecast?
options: Extending a line beyond the plotted points is not a recognised technique in geographical inquiry
A line graph shows change over time, so it cannot be used to make any statement about the future
Fifteen years is short enough that the trend may reflect natural variability rather than lasting change
Rainfall data are secondary data, and forecasts can only be made from primary fieldwork data
questions.explanation: Extrapolation assumes the conditions producing a trend will persist, so a forecast is only as reliable as the record behind it; 15 years of rainfall can easily be dominated by El Nino and La Nina cycles rather than a long-term shift. The tempting wrong option claims secondary data cannot support forecasts — in fact long-run secondary records from the Bureau of Meteorology are exactly what strengthens such a forecast. The cue is to judge the length and representativeness of the record, not its source.

questions.stem: A class plans to survey shoppers about food costs. Which approach is ethical?
options: Record what they say without telling them, since people behave naturally
Publish every respondent's name and address so readers can verify
Survey only shoppers who agree with the hypothesis, for consistency
Explain the purpose, ask permission before recording, keep it anonymous
questions.explanation: Ethical inquiry requires informed consent, honesty about purpose, and protection of participants' privacy, so people can decide freely whether to take part. Recording people without telling them may seem to produce more natural data, but collecting information without consent breaches participants' rights regardless of how useful the data is. Selecting only agreeable respondents is also a research fault, since it biases the sample rather than testing the hypothesis.

questions.stem: A shopper chooses certified fair trade coffee, which guarantees growers a minimum price. This choice most directly reflects the ethical value of:
options: comparative advantage, specialising in the goods a country can produce at lowest relative cost
intragenerational equity, a fairer share of benefits between producers and consumers living now
intergenerational equity, protecting the interests of people not yet born from today's decisions
national self-sufficiency, meeting a country's needs from its own production rather than imports
questions.explanation: Fair trade certification is about how the benefits of a trading relationship are distributed among people alive today, which is intragenerational equity. Intergenerational equity is tempting because fair trade schemes often include environmental conditions, but the minimum price itself is about present-day growers, not future generations. Comparative advantage and self-sufficiency are economic ideas about what a country produces, not ethical values about fairness.

questions.stem: After studying deforestation, a group concludes that Australia should ban all imports of a tropical crop grown mainly by smallholder farmers. Which criticism of this conclusion is a valid geographical and ethical one?
options: It is invalid because deforestation is an economic matter rather than an environmental issue for geographers
It is invalid because conclusions in geography must be based on fieldwork rather than on published sources
It overlooks interconnection: a ban would also remove the income that supports smallholders' wellbeing overseas
It is invalid because geographers should describe patterns only and never make judgements about issues
questions.explanation: Justifying a conclusion ethically means tracing who is affected, and interconnection shows that a consumer decision in Australia flows through to producers' livelihoods elsewhere, which a blanket ban would damage. The claim that geographers should never make judgements is wrong: weighing ethical values and perspectives is a required part of geographical inquiry. Deforestation is plainly an environmental issue, and secondary sources are legitimate evidence, so those criticisms are simply false.

questions.stem: A rural council proposes to cap how much groundwater irrigators may pump each year, arguing that the aquifer must still be usable by farming families in 50 years' time. Which ethical value most directly justifies this conclusion?
options: Economies of scale — costs per unit falling as production increases
Intergenerational equity — fairness towards people not yet born
Intragenerational equity — fairness between people alive at the same time
Comparative advantage — regions specialising in what they produce most cheaply
questions.explanation: The council's reasoning rests on protecting a resource for future users, and equity between present and future generations is exactly what intergenerational equity means. The tempting alternative, fairness between people alive at the same time, is the definition of intragenerational equity, which would apply if the argument were about sharing water fairly between irrigators and townspeople today. The cue is the time frame: 'in 50 years' time' or 'for future generations' signals intergenerational equity, while 'between groups now' signals intragenerational equity. Comparative advantage and economies of scale are economic concepts about production and cost, not ethical values about fairness.

questions.stem: After interviewing only the operators of a large irrigated cotton farm, a student concludes that 'expanding irrigation in the catchment is the fairest option for everyone'. Which criticism of this conclusion is the strongest on ethical and geographical grounds?
options: A claim about fairness to everyone is unsound because farm operators have no legitimate stake in the issue
A claim about fairness to everyone needs the perspectives of downstream users and Traditional Owners as well
A claim about fairness to everyone is invalid because interviews are always less reliable than statistics
A claim about fairness to everyone must be avoided because geographers describe places rather than judge them
questions.explanation: Justifying a conclusion about fairness requires weighing the values and perspectives of all groups affected at different points in the catchment, so evidence from only one stakeholder cannot support a claim about 'everyone'. The suggestion that interviews are always less reliable than statistics is false: interview data is a legitimate primary source, and the problem here is the narrow range of views, not the method. Geographers are expected to make reasoned ethical judgements, and farm operators are genuine stakeholders whose views belong in the analysis — they simply are not the only ones. The cue is the word 'everyone': check whether every affected group has actually been heard.

questions.stem: Judging a strategy against environmental criteria asks mainly whether it:
options: can be completed within the timeframe set by the government
maintains soil, water, vegetation and biodiversity long term
keeps the total cost of the project within the available budget
is accepted as fair by the different groups of people affected
questions.explanation: Environmental criteria judge a strategy by its effects on natural systems — soil health, water quality and quantity, vegetation cover and biodiversity. Keeping within budget is an economic criterion, not an environmental one, and is the most tempting swap because cost dominates most real decisions. Acceptance and fairness among affected groups is the social criterion. The cue: ask 'what does this measure — nature, money, or people?'

questions.stem: A class recommends that a coastal council build a rock seawall to protect a beachfront road. Which sentence best states a PREDICTED IMPACT of the strategy?
options: The seawall would be built from quarried granite blocks placed along the 600 metre road frontage
The council has already surveyed residents, and most say protecting the road is their highest priority
Seawalls are the most common form of hard engineering used on Australian urban coastlines
Within a decade the beach in front of the wall is likely to narrow, as reflected wave energy removes sand
questions.explanation: A predicted impact is a statement about consequences that would follow if the strategy went ahead, ideally with a timeframe and a mechanism — here, wave reflection scouring sand and narrowing the beach. Describing the granite blocks and the 600 metre frontage is a description of the strategy itself, which students often mistake for its impacts. Survey results are evidence of community attitudes, and the popularity of seawalls nationally is background context. Ask: does the sentence say what will happen as a result?

questions.stem: Two strategies for improving food security in a dryland farming region are scored against criteria. Strategy A scores highest on economic returns but lowest on environmental sustainability; Strategy B scores moderately on all three criteria. A group recommends Strategy B. Which justification is geographically strongest?
options: Strategy B is the safer choice because taking the middle option always reduces the risk of a strategy failing
Strategy B is better because a strategy must score equally on environmental, economic and social criteria to be valid
Strategy B is preferable because environmental criteria always outweigh economic criteria in geographical decision-making
Strategy B avoids a serious weakness on one criterion, so its benefits are more likely to be sustained beyond the short term
questions.explanation: A strong justification explains the trade-off: a strategy that fails badly on one criterion can undermine its own gains over time, so a balanced option may deliver more durable benefits. Claiming the middle option is always safer is a rule of thumb, not evidence, and is tempting because it reaches the same recommendation for the wrong reason. There is no requirement that scores be equal across criteria, and no rule ranks environmental criteria above economic ones — weightings depend on the place and the issue.

questions.stem: How should a geographical report acknowledge the research findings it relies on?
options: List every website visited at the end, without linking sources to claims
Cite only sources that disagree, since supporting evidence speaks for itself
Name the author, organisation and year in the text, with a reference list
Rewrite each source in your own words, since paraphrase needs no citation
questions.explanation: Acknowledging research findings means the reader can trace each claim back to the source that supports it, which requires in-text attribution plus full reference details. The idea that paraphrasing removes the need to cite is the most tempting error: changing the wording does not change whose findings they are, so the citation is still required. The cue is that acknowledgement is about the origin of the idea or data, not the exact words used.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about a proposed action is an EXPLANATION of the action rather than an evaluation of it?
options: Planting shelterbelts is the best option because it costs less per hectare than building windbreak fences
Planting shelterbelts is unsuitable here because the land taken out of production outweighs the yield gain
Planting shelterbelts rates poorly on social criteria because neighbouring farmers oppose the loss of cropping area
Planting shelterbelts of trees reduces wind speed across paddocks, which lowers soil erosion and evaporation
questions.explanation: An explanation sets out how and why an action works — here, the causal chain from reduced wind speed to less erosion and evaporation — without judging its worth. The cost comparison option is tempting because it also mentions the action and gives a reason, but words like 'best option' and a comparison against an alternative make it a judgement, that is, an evaluation. The cue is that explanations answer 'how does it work?' while evaluations answer 'how good is it?'

questions.stem: A Year 10 group recommends that their council fund free school breakfast programs in low-income suburbs to improve food security and wellbeing. Which piece of research evidence would most strengthen their evaluation of this proposed action?
options: A choropleth map showing which suburbs in the municipality have the highest rates of household food insecurity
Survey responses from students at the group's own school saying they would like a free breakfast to be provided
Published findings comparing attendance and concentration in schools that ran breakfast programs with similar schools that did not
A council media release stating that improving child wellbeing in disadvantaged suburbs is one of its strategic priorities
questions.explanation: Evaluating an action means judging whether it is likely to produce the intended outcome, so evidence that compares places where the action was taken with similar places where it was not gives the strongest test of effectiveness. The choropleth map of food insecurity is tempting, but it only establishes that a problem exists and where — it says nothing about whether breakfast programs fix it. Cue: evidence about the problem justifies acting, while evidence about outcomes evaluates the action.

questions.stem: A Year 10 group recommends that farmers in the Mallee adopt a soil-cover cropping method, supporting the recommendation with findings from a 2019 trial conducted on high-rainfall farms in coastal Victoria, which they cite in full. Which criticism of their use of the research is geographically strongest?
options: Findings from a high-rainfall coastal trial may not transfer to a low-rainfall inland region, so the evidence needs testing against Mallee conditions
Secondary data from a published trial cannot be used to support a recommendation, because only primary data collected by the group counts as evidence
Data gathered in 2019 is out of date and cannot be used, because geographical evidence must come from the most recent twelve months
Naming the source of the trial makes the recommendation biased, because a report should present findings without identifying who produced them
questions.explanation: Evidence must be judged for its relevance to the place being studied: rainfall, soils and evaporation differ sharply between coastal Victoria and the Mallee, so a result found in one environment may not hold in the other. The claim that only primary data counts is simply false — published secondary research is standard and valued in geographical inquiry, provided it is acknowledged. The other options invent rules that do not exist: there is no twelve-month limit on data, and naming a source is exactly what proper acknowledgement requires. The cue is transferability: always ask whether the study's location and conditions match your own.

questions.stem: In geography, a biome is best defined as:
options: a large-scale region defined by its distinctive climate, vegetation and associated animal life
a small local area of habitat, such as a wetland or a single patch of remnant bushland
a region defined by national borders and the food crops its government chooses to grow
a band of latitude defined only by average annual temperature, regardless of rainfall
questions.explanation: A biome is a very large region grouped by its climate and the vegetation type that climate supports, together with the animals adapted to it — examples include tropical rainforest, temperate grassland and tundra. The option describing a small habitat patch confuses a biome with an ecosystem or habitat, which operates at a much smaller scale. The cue is scale plus climate-vegetation: if the region is continental in size and named by its plant cover, it is a biome; if it is a local patch, it is an ecosystem.

questions.stem: The world's largest hot desert biomes, such as the Sahara and central Australia, are mostly found near 20°–30° north and south of the equator. The main reason is that:
options: at these latitudes air is rising rapidly, which carries all available moisture away from the surface
these latitudes receive the most direct overhead sunlight on Earth throughout the whole year
warm ocean currents along nearby coasts stop moist air from ever reaching inland areas
at these latitudes air is descending and warming, which suppresses cloud formation and rainfall
questions.explanation: Air that rose near the equator moves poleward and sinks around 20°–30°, and sinking air warms and dries, so cloud and rain rarely form — the classic subtropical high-pressure belts where hot deserts sit. The 'rising air' option reverses the process: rising air cools, condenses and produces rainfall, which is why the equatorial belt is wet, not dry. Link the words: rising air equals rain, sinking air equals desert.

questions.stem: A location records an average temperature of 24°C in its hottest month and 4°C in its coldest month, with about 500 mm of rainfall falling mainly in the cooler months. Its natural vegetation is tussock grasses with very few trees. Which biome is this?
options: Tropical rainforest
Tundra
Temperate grassland
Tropical savanna
questions.explanation: A large seasonal temperature range with a cold month, moderate rainfall of around 500 mm and grass-dominated vegetation with few trees are the signature features of temperate grassland. Tropical savanna is the tempting choice because it is also grassy with scattered trees, but savanna has no cold month and its rain falls in the hot season. Check the coldest month first: near 4°C rules out any tropical biome.

questions.stem: Temperate grassland biomes such as the Argentinian Pampas, the North American Prairies and parts of the Ukrainian steppe have been converted to grain cropping more extensively than almost any other biome. The main geographical reason is that these regions combine:
options: the highest rainfall totals on Earth with year-round warmth suited to continuous cropping
thin, acidic soils that need little cultivation before seed can be sown by machinery
a total absence of drought risk, which removes the need for irrigation or crop insurance
deep, nutrient-rich soils built up under grasses, flat land and enough rainfall for cereals
questions.explanation: Generations of grasses dying back added organic matter to produce deep, fertile soils, and combined with level terrain for machinery and moderate seasonal rainfall this makes temperate grasslands ideal for wheat, maize and other cereals. The 'highest rainfall on Earth with year-round warmth' option describes equatorial rainforest, not grassland — and those conditions are actually poorly suited to grain harvesting. The distinguishing cue is soil: grassland fertility is stored in the soil, unlike rainforest fertility, which is stored in the vegetation.

questions.stem: Tropical rainforests have the highest biomass productivity of any biome, yet land cleared for farming there often gives poor crop yields within a few years. Which explanation is correct?
options: Most nutrients are held in the living vegetation and recycled quickly, so cleared soils hold few nutrients and heavy rain leaches what remains
Most nutrients are stored deep in the soil profile, so cleared land stays fertile but cool temperatures slow the growth of food crops
Rainforest regions receive too little rainfall for crops once the tree canopy has been removed, so cleared land quickly becomes desert
Rainforest soils are deep and rich in nutrients, but the terrain in every rainforest region is far too steep for cropping machinery
questions.explanation: High biomass productivity in rainforests comes from constant warmth and rainfall driving rapid growth and rapid decomposition, but the nutrients cycle almost entirely through the living and decaying vegetation rather than being stored in the soil; once the trees are removed, the thin nutrient store is used up or washed away by heavy rain. The option claiming nutrients are stored deep in the soil reverses the actual nutrient cycle and also wrongly describes rainforest temperatures, which are consistently warm year-round. Rainfall is high, not low, after clearing, and while some rainforest land is steep, large areas such as the Amazon and Congo basins are low-lying. Cue: high biomass does not mean fertile soil — ask where the nutrients are stored.

questions.stem: Which pair of conditions most limits the area available for broadacre cropping in Australia?
options: Freezing winters combined with permanent snow across the inland plains
Steep terrain across most of the continent with year-round cloud cover
Low, variable rainfall combined with ancient soils low in nutrients
High reliable rainfall with young volcanic soils holding too much water
questions.explanation: Most of Australia is arid or semi-arid, and its soils are geologically very old and heavily weathered, so they are low in phosphorus and nitrogen; this is why cropping is concentrated in a crescent of moderate-rainfall land and why fertiliser use is essential. The option about young volcanic soils is tempting because Australia does have small areas of fertile basalt soils (such as parts of western Victoria and the Darling Downs), but these are exceptions, not the national pattern. The cue: think about why the 'wheat belt' forms a narrow arc rather than covering the whole continent — it is rainfall and soil fertility, not cold or slope.

questions.stem: A wheat grower decides to sow 400 hectares instead of the planned 700 hectares because global wheat prices have fallen while fertiliser, fuel and machinery costs have risen sharply. This decision is best classified as a response to:
options: Technological factors, because cheaper machinery would have allowed the full area to be sown
Political factors, because world prices for wheat are set each season by the Australian government
Economic factors, because the expected returns no longer cover the cost of inputs on the extra area
Environmental factors, because falling prices show that the soil can no longer support the extra area
questions.explanation: Input costs and commodity prices determine the profit margin per hectare, and this margin is what drives decisions about how much land to plant — a classic economic influence on crop production. The environmental option is tempting because area sown often does depend on soil moisture, but nothing in the scenario mentions soil or rainfall; the trigger given is prices and costs. Check what the scenario actually names as the cause before choosing a category.

questions.stem: In parts of the Murray–Darling Basin, decades of flood irrigation have caused watertables to rise and bring dissolved salts near the surface, reducing crop yields. This situation best illustrates that:
options: A technology that raises production in the short term can create an environmental constraint on later production
Salinity is a purely natural process, so irrigation technology has no influence on where salts accumulate
Irrigation always increases long-term yields, because added water dilutes any salts already in the soil
Salinity only affects crops grown on coastal land, where seawater can move inland through the soil
questions.explanation: Dryland and irrigation salinity occur when extra water moves past the root zone, lifting the watertable and mobilising salts stored in the soil profile; the technology that boosted yields becomes the cause of a later environmental limit. The claim that salinity is purely natural is tempting because Australia's soils do contain naturally stored salt, but the rate and location of salt accumulation are strongly changed by clearing and irrigation. The cue is the phrase 'watertables have risen' — that is a human-induced change to the water balance.

questions.stem: Which of these is an ENVIRONMENTAL factor limiting crop production, rather than an economic or technological one?
options: The depth and fertility of the topsoil in a cropping district
The price a grower is paid per tonne of grain at harvest
The availability of GPS-guided seeding machinery on the farm
The interest rate charged on a loan for new silo storage
questions.explanation: Environmental factors are the natural conditions of the place — climate, soil, landform, water availability — and soil depth and fertility are physical properties of the land. Grain price is tempting because it strongly affects how much is planted, but a price is set in markets, making it economic, not environmental. Cue: ask whether the factor would still exist if there were no farmers or markets at all; soil would, prices, machinery and loans would not.

questions.stem: Many Australian grain growers have shifted to no-till sowing with stubble left standing on the paddock. What is the main environmental sustainability benefit of this practice?
options: Soil is left covered and undisturbed, which cuts wind and water erosion and helps the soil hold moisture between rains
Crops can be grown continuously without any fertiliser, because undisturbed soil supplies all the nutrients a crop removes
Weeds are eliminated from the paddock, so growers no longer need to apply any herbicide during the season
Rainfall is prevented from soaking in, so the watertable stays low and salinity can never develop in the paddock
questions.explanation: No-till leaves the previous crop's stubble anchored on the surface, protecting bare soil from wind and raindrop impact and shading it so less moisture evaporates — both central to keeping the soil resource productive. The fertiliser option is the tempting one, because no-till does build soil organic matter over time, but harvested grain still removes nutrients that must be replaced. Remember that no-till manages soil structure, cover and moisture; it does not abolish nutrient budgets or weed control, and in fact no-till growers usually rely more on herbicides.

questions.stem: A farmer plants belts of native trees along paddock boundaries. What is the main ENVIRONMENTAL benefit?
options: It removes the need for fertiliser, because trees supply all crop nutrients
It raises the watertable, lifting stored salts up into the root zone
It guarantees higher grain prices, since buyers pay more for shaded paddocks
It reduces wind erosion of topsoil and gives habitat for native species
questions.explanation: Shelterbelts slow wind speed at ground level, which cuts topsoil loss and evaporation, and the strips of native vegetation give habitat and corridors for birds and insects — both environmental gains. Saying it removes the need for fertiliser is wrong: shelterbelts do not supply the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium that crops remove from soil. Note also that deep-rooted perennial vegetation lowers rather than raises watertables, which is why tree planting is used to combat dryland salinity, not cause it.

questions.stem: Which is a POLITICAL constraint on the capacity to feed future populations?
options: Rising soil salinity in irrigation districts lowering crop yields
Sharp increases in the price of fertiliser, fuel and machinery
Longer and more frequent droughts reducing grain harvest reliability
Armed conflict stopping planting and blocking transport to markets
questions.explanation: Political constraints come from governments, conflict and decision-making: war, trade restrictions, weak land tenure and poor governance all limit food production and distribution. Rising fertiliser, fuel and machinery prices is the most tempting alternative, but cost is an economic constraint, even though governments can influence prices. The cue is to ask what is doing the limiting: a decision or conflict (political), a price or market (economic), or the physical environment (environmental).

questions.stem: After a poor harvest, a major rice-exporting country bans rice exports to keep domestic prices low. World rice prices jump and import-dependent countries in Africa struggle to buy supplies. This situation best illustrates that:
options: export bans raise supply in importing countries by encouraging local farmers to plant more
political decisions about trade can restrict food access even when food physically exists elsewhere
world food output had fallen below the total amount of food humans need that year
food insecurity in importing countries is caused mainly by their own soil and climate limits
questions.explanation: An export ban does not destroy any food; it changes who can legally buy it, showing that governance and trade policy are constraints on food security separate from how much is produced. The option about world output falling below human needs is tempting, but a single country's poor harvest and ban does not mean global production was insufficient — the grain existed but could not move. The cue is to ask whether the shortage came from less food existing or from barriers to reaching people.

questions.stem: Global agriculture currently produces enough kilojoules for the whole human population, yet hundreds of millions of people remain undernourished. Which explanation of this is correct?
options: Global averages hide the fact that world production is actually below total human requirements
Food security depends on access, affordability and distribution, not only on the total quantity grown
Undernourishment happens only where drought or poor soils make local farming impossible
Roughly enough food is grown, but almost all losses and waste occur in low-income countries
questions.explanation: Food security has several dimensions — availability, access, affordability, utilisation and stability — so people can go hungry in a world of adequate total production if they cannot afford or physically reach food. The option blaming drought and poor soils alone is tempting because environmental limits are real, but undernourishment also occurs where food is abundant and incomes or infrastructure are lacking. Food loss and waste are also substantial in high-income countries, largely at the retail and household stage.

questions.stem: How is climate change projected to constrain the world's capacity to feed itself?
options: Only tropical countries face lower yields; temperate zones are unaffected
Higher carbon dioxide removes the need for irrigation, as crops use less
More frequent droughts and heatwaves are projected to lower yields
Warmer air raises yields everywhere, since all crops grow faster when warm
questions.explanation: Climate change constrains food production mainly by increasing the frequency and severity of heat extremes, drought and erratic rainfall, all of which cut yields and raise the risk of harvest failure in major grain belts, including Australia's. The claim that warming raises yields everywhere is tempting because modest warming can extend growing seasons in a few cool, high-latitude areas, but heat above a crop's tolerance and reduced water availability lower yields overall — 'every region' and 'all crops' make the statement false. The cue: a real constraint is stated as increased variability and risk, not as a benefit applied universally.

questions.stem: Most projections state that the extra food needed by 2050 will have to come mainly from raising yields on land already farmed, rather than from clearing large areas of new cropland. Which reason best explains this?
options: International agreements legally prohibit every country from converting any additional land to agricultural production
Crop yields have already reached their absolute biological maximum, so no further yield increases are physically possible
Most remaining uncleared land is too dry, steep or infertile to crop, or holds forests whose clearing would worsen climate change
There is essentially no uncleared land left anywhere on Earth, so every possible hectare is already under crops or pasture
questions.explanation: The land not yet farmed is largely marginal — arid, steep, saline or thin-soiled — or is forest and savanna whose clearing releases stored carbon and destroys habitat, so expansion is both agronomically poor and environmentally costly. Saying no uncleared land remains is the closest distractor, but large areas of forest and rangeland could physically be cleared; the constraint is that doing so is unproductive or environmentally damaging, not that the land does not exist. Look for constraints framed as environmental quality and trade-offs rather than as absolute physical or legal impossibility.

questions.stem: Refrigerated shipping containers and air freight have allowed Australian supermarkets to stock fresh mangoes, berries and salmon all year round. The term geographers use for the distance food travels from producer to consumer is:
options: Food security
Food sovereignty
Food footprint
Food miles
questions.explanation: Food miles refers specifically to the distance food is transported between where it is produced and where it is finally consumed, and is often used when discussing the emissions of long-distance freight. Food security is the tempting alternative, but it means reliable access by all people to sufficient, affordable, nutritious food, not a measure of transport distance. If the statement is about kilometres travelled, it is food miles; if it is about whether people can get enough to eat, it is food security.

questions.stem: A Wangaratta furniture maker begins selling through an online marketplace and ships orders by courier to customers across Australia and New Zealand. Which statement best describes the geographical effect of these transport and digital changes on the business?
options: Its market area is unchanged, because online selling only shifts which local customers buy from it
Its market area has shrunk, because online competitors will always undercut a regional producer
Its market area has expanded well beyond the local region, so the friction of distance now matters less to sales
Its market area has expanded, which means the local region no longer influences its production costs at all
questions.explanation: Cheap parcel freight and online platforms reduce the friction of distance — the way distance discourages interaction — so a small producer can reach distant customers it could never have served from a shopfront. The claim that the local region no longer influences costs at all is tempting because expansion is real, but the maker still depends on local timber, labour, rent and road access, so place still matters. Watch for absolute words like 'at all' and 'always'; interconnection reduces the barrier of distance rather than erasing local geography.

questions.stem: Since fast broadband and video-conferencing became widespread, several coastal and inland Victorian towns have recorded population growth as city workers move in and work remotely. Which pair of consequences for those towns is best supported by evidence of this trend?
options: Rising house prices alongside a decline in demand for all local retail and hospitality businesses
Falling house prices alongside a decline in the town's need for any road or utility upgrades
Rising house prices alongside increased demand for local services such as childcare and health care
Falling house prices alongside increased demand for local services such as childcare and health care
questions.explanation: When digital connectivity lets people keep city incomes while living regionally, extra demand for housing pushes prices and rents up, and the larger resident population increases pressure on local services and infrastructure. The version with falling house prices plus rising service demand is internally inconsistent: more in-migration cannot reduce competition for housing. The cue is to check that both halves of the option follow from the same cause — population growth raises demand for housing and for services together.

questions.stem: What does 'biodiversity' mean?
options: The total number of animals in an area
The area of land set aside as parkland
The rate at which a forest regrows
The variety of living things in an area
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of life — species, genes and ecosystems — not simply how many individuals are present. A place can hold huge numbers of one species and still have low biodiversity.
questions.teaching:
The word combines "biological" and "diversity", and the second half is the part that matters.

It measures variety rather than quantity, and it works at several levels: the number of different species in an area, the genetic variation within each species, and the range of ecosystems present. A wheat paddock can hold millions of individual plants and have very low biodiversity, while a patch of remnant bushland next to it has far fewer plants and far more. Australia is one of seventeen megadiverse countries, with a high proportion of species found nowhere else — which is why habitat loss here matters globally.

questions.stem: What is deforestation?
options: The seasonal loss of leaves from a forest
The permanent clearing of forest for other uses
The natural death of trees in a mature forest
The planting of trees on previously bare land
questions.explanation: Deforestation is forest cleared and converted to another land use, usually farming or building. Planting trees on bare land is afforestation — the opposite move, and the tempting mirror-image answer.
questions.teaching:
The key word in this term is permanence: it means forest cleared and the land converted to something else, usually agriculture, grazing, mining or building.

That distinguishes it from logging where forest regrows, and from natural disturbance like fire in an adapted ecosystem. The consequences run in several directions at once: habitat and species lost, carbon released from the trees and soil, and less rainfall recycled back into the atmosphere. The reverse process, planting trees where forest did not recently stand, is afforestation, and restoring forest that was cleared is reforestation. Those opposite terms are the tempting near-misses.

questions.stem: What does 'sustainability' mean?
options: Using resources so they last for future generations
Using the cheapest resources available right now
Leaving an environment completely untouched
Replacing natural resources with manufactured ones
questions.explanation: Sustainability means meeting present needs without stopping future generations meeting theirs. It is tempting to read it as 'never touch anything', but sustainable use is still use.
questions.teaching:
The standard definition comes from the 1987 Brundtland Report: meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

Two things follow from that. First, it is about use continuing indefinitely, not about leaving everything untouched — a forest can be harvested sustainably if it regrows as fast as it is cut. Second, it is usually broken into three strands that have to be balanced: environmental, economic and social. A scheme that protects an ecosystem while destroying the livelihood of the community depending on it is not generally counted as sustainable, which is why the concept is contested in practice.

questions.stem: What is human wellbeing usually measured by?
options: Distance from the equator in kilometres
Health, education and income
Total population size alone
Land area available per person
questions.explanation: Wellbeing measures such as the Human Development Index combine health, education and income, because no single figure captures how well people live. Population size says nothing about wellbeing at all.
questions.teaching:
Income alone turns out to be a poor measure of how well people live, which is why composite indexes exist.

The Human Development Index, published by the UN, combines three strands: how long people live, how much education they get, and what income they have. Combining them catches cases a single figure misses — an oil-rich state with high income but poor health outcomes, or a poorer country with excellent schooling and life expectancy. Population size is not part of it at all, and neither is geography. Other measures such as the Gini coefficient add inequality, since averages can hide enormous gaps.

questions.stem: What is a renewable resource?
options: One that exists in extremely large quantities
One that can be recycled after it is used
One found in more than one country
One that replenishes within a human lifetime
questions.explanation: A renewable resource is replaced naturally on a human timescale — sunlight, wind, timber. Being plentiful is not the same thing: coal is abundant but takes millions of years to form.
questions.teaching:
The test is about rate, not abundance: is the resource replaced as fast as, or faster than, we use it, on a human timescale?

Sunlight, wind, flowing water and geothermal heat all pass easily. Timber and fish are more interesting — they are renewable in principle, but only if harvested no faster than they regenerate, which is why overfishing can effectively exhaust a "renewable" stock. Coal, oil and gas fail the test regardless of how much remains, because they take hundreds of millions of years to form. Note that renewable and low-emission are separate questions, even though they often coincide.

questions.stem: What does 'land degradation' mean?
options: A decline in the land's capacity to support life
A fall in the market value of farmland in a region
The conversion of farmland into housing
The natural erosion of a river valley
questions.explanation: Land degradation is a loss of the land's productive capacity — salinity, erosion, loss of soil structure. It is a physical change rather than a financial one, which is why the market-value option is wrong.
questions.teaching:
This describes a physical decline in what land can support, and Australia has several severe forms of it.

Salinity is the classic Australian case: clearing deep-rooted native vegetation lets the watertable rise, bringing salt to the surface where it kills crops. Erosion strips topsoil that took thousands of years to form. Compaction from stock and machinery stops water soaking in. Overgrazing removes the cover holding soil together. All of these reduce the land's productive capacity, which is the definition. It is a physical change rather than a financial one, so a fall in land prices does not count.

questions.stem: What is a catchment?
options: The total amount of water a dam can hold
The part of a river where it reaches the sea
The area a city draws its workers from
The area of land that drains into one river
questions.explanation: A catchment is all the land whose runoff drains to a single river or reservoir. What happens anywhere in it affects the water, which is why rivers are managed by catchment rather than by council boundary.
questions.teaching:
Water does not respect council boundaries, and this concept is why river management is organised the way it is.

It describes all the land whose rainfall and runoff drains towards a single river, lake or reservoir, separated from neighbouring ones by ridges of higher ground. Anything happening anywhere within it can affect the water downstream — fertiliser washing off a paddock, sediment from a building site, a factory discharge. The Murray-Darling Basin is the largest in Australia, covering about a seventh of the continent across four states, which is exactly why managing it requires agreement between governments.

questions.stem: What does 'urbanisation' mean?
options: The spread of farms into former bushland
The building of new roads between towns
A rise in the total population of a country
A growing share of people living in cities
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the shift of population from rural areas into towns and cities, measured as a share rather than a raw count. A country's population can grow without urbanising at all.
questions.teaching:
This is measured as a proportion rather than a raw number, and that distinction is what most questions test.

It describes a rising share of a country's population living in towns and cities rather than rural areas, driven by people moving for work and services and by cities growing naturally. A country's total population can grow substantially without urbanising at all, if rural and urban areas grow at the same rate. Australia is among the most urbanised countries on Earth, with roughly 86% of people in urban areas and most of those concentrated in a handful of coastal cities.

questions.stem: What is salinity in Australian farmland?
options: A shortage of water in the soil
A loss of topsoil to the wind
An excess of nitrogen fertiliser
A build-up of salt in the soil
questions.explanation: Clearing deep-rooted native vegetation lets the watertable rise and carry salt to the surface, where it damages crops. Loss of topsoil to wind is erosion, a different form of degradation.
questions.teaching:
This is one of the most serious forms of land degradation in Australia, and the mechanism is worth understanding because it is not obvious.

Salt has always been present deep in the soil profile, left by ancient seas and carried in by rain over millennia. Deep-rooted native vegetation used enough water to keep the watertable well below the surface. Clearing that vegetation for crops and pasture reduced water use, so the watertable rose, dissolving the stored salt and bringing it up into the root zone — and in places to the surface, where it forms visible white crusts and kills everything. Irrigation can cause the same effect by adding water.

questions.stem: What does an ecosystem include?
options: Living things and their environment
Only the plants in an area
Only the animals in an area
Only the soil and rock
questions.explanation: An ecosystem covers the organisms together with the non-living surroundings they depend on, and the interactions between them. Leaving out either half misses the point of the word.
questions.teaching:
The word covers more than the organisms, and that is the point of having it as a separate term from "community".

It means all the living things in an area together with the non-living surroundings they depend on — soil, water, air, sunlight, temperature — and, crucially, the interactions between all of them. Energy flows through it from the sun via producers to consumers, and nutrients cycle round. Defining it that way is what makes it useful: it explains why removing one species or changing the water flow can have effects far from the obvious point of impact.

questions.stem: What is an introduced species?
options: One found only in one country
One brought to an area by people
One that evolved in the area
One that has become extinct
questions.explanation: Introduced species arrive through human activity, deliberately or accidentally — rabbits and cane toads in Australia. A species found only in one place is endemic, which is the tempting near-term.
questions.teaching:
These arrive through human activity rather than by natural spread, sometimes deliberately and sometimes by accident.

Australia has a long list. Rabbits were released for hunting in 1859 and reached plague numbers within decades. Cane toads were introduced in 1935 to control a beetle, failed at that, and spread across the north. Foxes, cats, camels, blackberry and lantana all arrived the same way. Not all become pests — wheat and sheep are introduced too — but those that do are called invasive. The opposite term is endemic, meaning found naturally in one place and nowhere else, which is the tempting near-miss.

questions.stem: What is 'liveability'?
options: How many people currently live in a place
How large a city's area is
How old a settlement is
How well a place meets residents' needs
questions.explanation: Liveability judges how well somewhere supports the people living there — housing, transport, safety, green space. Population size says nothing about quality of life, which is the trap.
questions.teaching:
This measures how well a place supports the people who live there, and it is deliberately about quality rather than quantity.

Indexes typically weigh access to housing, healthcare, education, transport, employment, green space, safety, and environmental quality such as air and noise. Melbourne has repeatedly ranked near the top of global lists using measures like these. The judgement is partly subjective and depends on who is doing the ranking — a place that scores well for a professional couple may score badly for a family on a low income. Population size tells you nothing about it, which is what makes that option wrong.

questions.stem: What does a choropleth map use to show data?
options: Arrows showing movement
Shading or colour across areas
Dots placed at each recorded site
Lines joining equal values
questions.explanation: A choropleth shades whole areas by value, so darker usually means more. Dot maps and flow maps show the same kind of data in different ways, which is why each wrong option is a real map type.
questions.teaching:
Several map types show statistical data and each uses a different visual device, so the fastest way to tell them apart is to ask what is being varied.

This one varies colour or shading across defined areas — states, council districts, countries — with darker usually meaning a higher value. It suits data already collected by region, such as population density or unemployment. Other types vary something else: dot maps place a mark for each occurrence, proportional symbol maps vary the size of a circle, isoline maps join points of equal value, and flow maps use arrows for movement. Each wrong option here names a real technique.

questions.stem: What is the 'scale' of a map?
options: The ratio of map distance to real distance
The direction of north as marked on the page
The key explaining the symbols
The title given to the map
questions.explanation: Scale tells you how much the ground has been shrunk to fit the page, so it is what lets you convert a measured distance into a real one. Direction and key are separate map elements.
questions.teaching:
Maps have several standard elements, and it helps to name them all: title, orientation, legend, scale, source. Questions often test which is which.

The one asked about here tells you how much the ground has been shrunk to fit the page, expressed as a ratio like 1:100,000, as a statement, or as a marked bar. It is what lets you convert a measured distance on the map into a real one. Orientation is the north arrow, and the legend explains the symbols. A large-scale map covers a small area in fine detail; a small-scale map covers a large area coarsely, which sounds backwards until you think of it as a fraction.
